subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF LAWYER AND MEMBER'S STAFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently my office received representations from a constituent who was having difficulty getting a cheque out of the Department of Supply and Services. My constituent was represented by a local lawyer who prepared the submission and delivered it personally on October 29, 1985, to Mr. Lloyd Spiro, who is a counsel for legal services in the Department of Supply and Services. Following the submission, my constituent received word from Mr. Spiro saying that she would have a cheque by December 27, 1985, and then December 27 became February 1, 1986.
Out of frustration my constituent came to my office. One of my staff contacted Mr. Spiro's office. But, before returning my secretary's call, Mr. Spiro called my constituent's lawyer and was absolutely livid and rude. Then Mr. Spiro undertook to call my office and proceeded to call my constituent's lawyer a liar on several occasions and said that he would love to punch him in the mouth. During his tirade on the telephone to my secretary, Mr. Spiro accused my constituent's lawyer of misconstruing everything, and made some very degrading statements about him.
The point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, is that a public servant who acts in this manner does not deserve to be employed in the Public Service of Canada, and I am requesting that the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Mclnnes) take action. There is no way I will tolerate any member of my staff or a decent hard-working constituent having to put up with this kind of conduct and verbal abuse. The very least that I can expect is an apology to my secretary and to the lawyer concerned.

Mr. Speaker, the closure this month of B.C. Marine Shipbuilders, the oldest shipyard in British Columbia, terminates 250 permanent jobs
in Vancouver East. The campaign promise of the Conservative Government to revitalize our shipbuilding industry was another betrayal. The only concrete action the Government has taken has been a complete elimination of all Government support for this once thriving industry. A workforce which once boasted 15,000 jobs for skilled workers across Canada will dwindle to 5,000 by the end of this year. On the West Coast, B.C. Marine Shipbuilders will be the third shipyard in three months to cease operations.
Instead of taking action to save these jobs, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) have ignored telegrams and letters requesting immediate meetings and clear answers on policy direction. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankow-ski) has made a complete mockery of the Government's promise to aid shipbuilding by failing to ensure that two new CN ferries planned for the East Coast are built in Canada. Although he told the House in November, 1984, that these ferries will be built here, he is now considering using foreign-built ships at a cost of 10,000 person years to Canadian workers.
I urge the Government to act now to save our shipbuilding industry. Go West and meet with the people in the industry. Ensure Government support so that ships operated in Canada are built and serviced by Canadians. Give back to those proud and skilled workers their jobs.

Mr. Speaker, Census Day in Canada is rapidly approaching. However, the Conservative Government is threatening its accuracy by eliminating all funding for media advertising. Historically upwards of 2 per cent of Canadians are officially omitted from this statisticsgathering process, while unofficial reports claim the figure is significantly higher. A very worrisome statistic, however, is that of those omitted the majority are Canadians from ethnocultural communities. It stands to reason that without media advertising, including the important third language media outlets across the country, these numbers will inflate dramatically. That would indeed be most unfortunate.
Third language newspapers and magazines are widely followed, as are multilingual television and radio programming. In addition, ads placed in these media tend to offer greater prominence and therefore greater value for the advertising dollar, and better communication. I therefore urge the Minister responsible for Multiculturalism to urge his colleague, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Mclnnes) at the very least to approve census advertising in Canada's third language media. It is vital that our national statistics accurately depict the real and contemporary Canada, including the integral and inseparable multicultural components.
Mr. Speaker, 211 Progressive Conservative Members of Parliament were elected because we promised jobs, jobs, jobs. Today's figures from Stats-Canada have proven that we can deliver, deliver, deliver.
Hear, hear!

Not only has the rate of unemployment dropped across Canada to 9.8 per cent, the lowest in five years, but my home Province of British Columbia saw one of the biggest drops in the rate of unemployment of any province. Under a job-intensive Progressive Conservative Government the B.C. unemployment rate has gone from 15.2 per cent in 1984 to 12.9 per cent today. That is down 1.2 per cent in the last month alone. To put it in human terms, tens of thousands of British Columbians who were not working before the last election are working today.
There is an old saying that at a party the host sees the glass as half-full but the guest sees it as half-empty. Applying that philosophy to our job-creation figures, to the pessimist 9.8 per cent of Canadians are unemployed, but to the optimist over 90 per cent of Canadians are working.
However, beyond partisan pride I think every Member in this House is encouraged by today's figures. They mean that hundreds of thousands of Canadians who ask for nothing more than the feeling of accomplishment that comes from meaningful work have come through a horrible recession and bounced back into the workforce. Obviously there is more to be done. We want more Canadians working. However, today we acknowledge that we are well on our way to recovery and that the Government is fulfilling its mandate with jobs, jobs, jobs.

subsubtopic: VISITS BY UNITED STATES VESSELS ARMED WITH NUCLEAR WEAPONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians should not be surprised that the number of visits by American ships carrying nuclear weapons increased in the last two years, but this increase makes news in Canada, and that tells me that something is very wrong in the country. Canadians really have no idea of the extent to which their country is tied into the nuclear weapons race. They like to think that Canada is nuclear weapons-free because our forces do not actually have their fingers on the button. However, this is not true.
Nuclear weapons are anchored in Canadian ports, tethered to our docks by a few feet of rope, overflying our air space in B-52 bombers, and making test runs a few feet under the surface of our waters and a few hundred feet over Alberta and the Northwest Territories. Other nuclear weapons are ear-
February 7, 1986

marked to be sent to Canada in times of crisis. Canadians are either unaware of these facts or are ignoring them because their implications are too horrible to face. However, Canadians must face up to these facts if we are ever to deal effectively with the question of nuclear arms control and disarmament.
Governments, both Liberals and Conservative, have been guilty of keeping Canadians in the dark on nuclear issues. It serves their political purposes to avoid this controversy by hiding nuclear weapons agreements and asserting that Canada is nuclear free. This claim rings false to those who control the nuclear arsenals and know of our complicity in their deployment. Neither Moscow nor Washington will ever take seriously our plea that they cut their nuclear forces as long as we aid and abet the nuclear arms race.

subsubtopic: LOCATION OF NEW UNITED STATES EMBASSY IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada has embarked on a policy of selling the Crown jewels. First it was the threat of logging national parks, then selling our national aircraft manufacturer, then the possibility of privatizing Air Canada, and, finally, the potential sale of part of Mile Circle Park right here in the city of Ottawa to build a U.S. embassy.
This park is bordered by a residential neighbourhood. Hundreds of average Canadians live there and hundreds of children go to school there. It is the worst possible site for such a building. In the past American embassies have been the targets of very unfortunate events. Could the safety of innocent people living in the area be affected by the potential construction of such a structure in their neighbourhood?
As the opposition critic for the Department of Public Works, I call upon the Government to reject any American offers to buy or lease Mile Circle Park. I call on the Government to send a clear signal that Canadian parklands, our natural treasures, are not for sale. I call upon the Government to state clearly that it will not act improperly by selling Mile Circle Park or locating an embassy in it.

PAYMENT OF PREMIUMS BY ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Why are members of the Canadian Armed Forces forced to pay unemployment insurance premiums at a time when they do not qualify to collect benefits when they retire, because of changes made in the UIC regulations by the Government?

subtopic: PAYMENT OF PREMIUMS BY ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that is a question that the same Hon. Member put to my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, just yesterday. Oh, that is right, the Hon. Member bumbled when he asked the question. I forgot that.
The answer to the question is quite simply that these changes were announced in November, 1984. They have been referred to the Forget Commission because it is a very complex issue. It is something which will impact not only on the people in the Armed Forces but on others who might be taking early

February 7, 1986
Oral Questions
retirement as well. The Hon. Member's concern is well noted and the Forget Commission will be giving us some good advice on this matter, I am sure.

Mr. Speaker, will the Minister stick to the subject matter and explain to this House and to all Canadians why the Government changed the unemployment insurance regulations, which have virtually denied the right of former members of the Canadian Armed Forces to collect benefits therefrom, and then, after the fact, it appointed a commission to review the Unemployment Insurance Program? Why did the Government not wait until at least its own commission had reported? It changed the regulations and then it asks someone to review the whole thing.

Mr. Speaker, there are a very wide range of issues which have been referred to the Forget Commission, not just the single issue referred to by the Hon. Member. We have not had a full review of the unemployment insurance system for a number of years now-
It was 1981.

-and a lot of changes have occurred in the system. There have been changes in a number of social programs to assist people who are out of work, and there have been changes in the economic environment in which people are living and working.
It was because of all of these things that we felt, in the middle of last year, that it was very important that we refer the whole question of unemployment insurance to the Forget Commission. I would ask the Hon. Member to watch for the results of this Commission and to give us some advice when the Commission comes down with its report.

Mr. Speaker, this is a question which I will take as notice and refer to my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board. The Hon. Member and the President of the Treasury Board have had a number of discussions on this subject, I know, and 1 am sure the matter will be considered and discussed with the Hon. Member within a very short time.

Mr. Speaker, is the Minister aware of the fact that a number of his colleagues from the Conservative Caucus have in fact raised this question in the House of Commons? Mr. Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board was in the House yesterday. I am sure he will be in the House next Monday or Tuesday. I would think it would be far more appropriate for the Hon. Member to refer that question to the Minister who is responsible for this particular issue.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question from the Official Opposition House Leader. I would like to take this opportunity to outline the Business of the House for the next several days.
As you are aware, the first item of business today will be second reading of Bill C-93, an Act relating to the establishment of self-government for the Sechelt Indian Band. Following that we will resume consideration of Bill C-90, an Act respecting pension plans. If the debate on Bill C-90 concludes, the next item of business will be resumption of second reading debate on Bill C-45 concerning the creation of unions on Parliament Hill.
On Monday the first item of business will be Bill C-80, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act at third reading. If that debate is completed, the House will move to Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976, which is at report stage.
On Tuesday the focus of debate will be House of Commons reform. Following extensive consultations with Members from all sides, yesterday I tabled a revised package of proposed Standing Orders and a Notice of Motion which seeks to implement the proposed rules for a trial period commencing with the return of the House following the February recess and ending on the last sitting day of this year. I hope that after Members have had the opportunity to register their views in debate the House will take up the challenge of reform and agree to what I believe would be a very constructive experiment.
February 7, 1986

In the event that debate wraps up early, and in keeping with the other reform initiatives, the backup to the debate on the proposed Standing Orders will be Government Order No. 71. That order is the motion referring to the paper entitled Lobbying and the Registration of Paid Lobbyists: A Discussion Paper to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization for their consideration and recommendations.
Finally, I hope that we will have made sufficient progress by Wednesday to call Bill C-86, an Act to amend the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. If that debate is completed it would be my intention to commence consideration of Bill C-92, an Act to regulate interests in petroleum in relation to frontier lands, which is at second reading.

speakeroldname: Hon. David Crombie (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: SECHELT INDIAN BAND SELF-GOVERNMENT ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-93, An Act relating to the establishment of self-government for the Sechelt Indian Band, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
He said: Mr. Speaker, today I rise to ask all Hon. Members to consider legislation that will restore self-governing rights to the Sechelt Indian community of British Columbia. Moreover, the proposed legislation will demonstrate the Government's commitment to advancing self-government for all Indian people and thereby advance the cause of Canada.
I believe that this legislation is in the best tradition of Canadian federalism, demonstrating creative flexibility and power sharing not only for the benefit of the Sechelt community but for the country as a whole.
There was a time when all Indian nations had self-governing powers in this country, those very powers which Canadians enjoy today, but which they very often take for granted. These self-governing powers, the most basic of all human rights, were taken away from Indian people. But today with this legislation we have the opportunity to recognize those rights of self-government again, at least for one Indian community.
This proposed Act will catch the interest and I hope the imagination of native people all over the country. Canadians in general and, I can assure some, indigenous people the world over.
As I have already mentioned, self-government is not new to Indian people. In fact, finally there is a growing realization in this country that Indian culture has been fundamental to the growth of democratic and political institutions in this country. Those who are familiar with the rich Indian heritage will know that various forms of Government existed among Indian nations in this country for centuries. What better example, and perhaps one of the best known, than the formation of the League of the Iroquois, inspired by Hiawatha around 1570.
That confederacy over 400 years ago, which consisted of the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca and later, the Tuscarora, exerted a dominant political and millitary influence throughout eastern North America for more than 200 years.
The political and social structure of that League, its emphasis on an equal voice for all members of the confederacy, its respect for human dignity and its emphasis on rights, obligations and participation has remained an enduring legacy in this country for those who have the wit to look at it. I could mention scores of other examples, from sea to sea to sea, which act as historical beacons for Indian people in their quest for the renewal of self-government in our own time.
For the broader public, self-government for Indian people has raised interest, support and a lot of questions. How will it be worked out? What will it mean in practice?
I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), in his opening remarks at the First Ministers Conference on Aboriginal Rights on April 2, 1985, put the situation very well when he said:
We Canadians are a cautious people and self-government is a term which is worrisome to some of us. But self-government is not something that I fear. It is not an end in itself, but rather a means to reach common goals.
He said:
The federal Government's approach to self-government for aboriginal peoples takes account of these realities, of the inventiveness and creativity that Canadians have always shown in developing their democratic institutions. It is through self-government that a people can maintain the sense of pride and self-worth which is necessary to productive, happy lives.
The Sechelt proposal gives us one set of answers to what self-government can mean to one community and how it may be worked out for other communities. But even as this Parliament works to afford the Sechelt concept the recognition of law, I can assure you that there are hundreds of Indian communities right now who are fashioning their own forms of self-government and who will be looking for our support in the very near future.
They include the Swampy Cree in northwestern Manitoba; the Nishawbe-Aski Nation representing Cree and Ojibway people in northern Ontario; the Kahnawake; the Akwesasne; the Tyendinaga community proposal on Mohawk self-government; Pointe-Bleue in the Province of Quebec; the Enoch band in Alberta; the Kootenay Indian Area Council representing five communities in the interior of British Columbia, the Robinson Treaty Nation proposal submitted through the Union of Ontario Indians; the Pas band in Manitoba; the Yellowhead Tribal Council; the Sushwap Nation of British Columbia; the Caribou Tribal Council and so many, many others.
Of course, a number of Members in this Chamber will know that self-government arrangements have been tried before. In 1984, through the James Bay and northern Quebec land claim settlement, the self-government aspirations of the Cree and Naskapi peoples of northern Quebec were given recognition in law by the House. I am looking forward to an implementation plan that will match the imagination of that understanding.
February 7, 1986

The current push for self-government emerged from a well known history of discontent. After Canada's national Government took shape in 1867, it was the Indian agents who controlled a large part of Indian life. In the last 20 years, Government tried to turn over more management to Indian people, but usually kept the final say for itself.
Indian people now want to put on their own face and their own stamp on their own Government. Here is one Indian community which wants to chart its own course, to plan its future and turn its dream into reality. However, I can assure you again that it is a vision that is shared by all Indian communities in this country.
When Parliament's Special Committee on Indian Self-Government in Canada held hearings in 1983, Indian native people from all parts of the country said that they wanted two main changes. First, they wanted a new and more self-reliant relationship with the federal Government; second, a better and stronger economic base.
Both these goals involve more community power to determine their own membership; to control such matters as health, education and social services, to manage their own economic enterprises and their own lands and to determine the form of Government under which they will live.
Today, some communities are eager and some are cautious. Some want one approach and some another. However, everyone agrees on one thing-that the time has come to establish Indian self-government in Canada.
All Parties in the House endorsed the recommendations of that Special Committee. The Government has accepted that report as the important fundamental document from which Indian self-government will proceed. That is why the Government has taken a community-based approach to self-government because it means that Indian people can tailor their own form of Government, one suited to their own circumstances, which reflects their own past and one in which they can mould their own future.
There are many forms of self-government, many degrees of self-sufficiency and many dimensions of self-determination. It might take place by legislation, by new funding arrangements that transfer responsibility, in conjunction with native claim settlements, or by a maximum use of by-law powers in the present Indian Act.
Our concept is a simple one. Instead of making communities fit our legislation, we will make legislation that fits the community. Self-government will be more than the end result; it will also be part of the process. Working in this way, Indian people can build self-government at their own pace and according to their own lights.
But who are these Indian people? What sort of people are
they?
I think my colleague and friend, the right Hon. Member for Yellowhead, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) described very eloquently who they are. He was
Sechelt Indian Band Self-Government Act
participating in the debate in this House nearly one year ago when we were amending the Indian Act with Bill C-31. The changes this Government introduced, which he so vigorously supported and which this House endorsed at that time, provided for equality of men and women under the Act and a measure of self-government by giving Indian communities the power to control their membership. During that debate he put it this way:
The children of the Eden Valley Reserve west of my home town were as free as I was to run, to ride and to be children. However, when we stopped being children, the youngsters of Eden Valley were not as free to be themselves as the youngsters of High River because to be Indian in the land which the Stoneys, the Blackfoot and the Cree discovered was to have your life run by someone else. There is somewhat more freedom now for the Stoneys, the Cree and the Blackfoot, but their memory and our legacy was of Ottawa running Indian lives, Ottawa setting Indian standards.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me look at the specifics of the Bill by which we are untying the strings.
After many discussions with the Sechelt people and the B.C. Government, we have agreed on a form of enabling legislation. Instead of a skeleton framework that leaves everything too vague, or an exhaustive agreement that sets too many rules, this legislation will let various new powers come into place over time, subject to negotiation within certain clearly defined parameters.
The enabling legislation sets up the community as a legal entity with all the capacities, rights, powers and privileges of a natural person. With this legislation, the Sechelt community may enter into contracts and agreements; acquire and hold property; sell and dispose of property; expend, invest or borrow money.
Under this legislation, the community will develop its own written constitution, a document which will be the fundamental cornerstone of its government. Under the constitution, the community can establish the composition of the Council, its terms of office and tenure of its members; establish procedures or processes to be followed by council in exercising the band's powers and carrying out its duties; provide for a system of financial accountability of the council to the members of the band; include a membership code for the band; establish rules and procedures to be followed in respect of the disposition of interests in Sechelt lands; set out specific legislative powers of the council and provide for any other matters relating to the Government of the band, its members or its lands.
This brings us, Mr. Speaker, to the legislative powers of the council. I will note some of those things, but the list is obviously not exhaustive.
The council will have the power to make laws in relation to matters coming within any of the selected classes of matters to the extent that it is authorized by the constitution of the band: access to and residence on Sechelt lands; zoning and land use planning; expropriation for community purposes; use, construction, maintenance, repair and demolition of buildings; taxation for local purposes of interests in Sechelt lands and of occupants and tenants of Sechelt lands, including assessment, collection and enforcement procedures and appeals; administration and management of property belonging to the band;

February 7, 1986
Sechelt Indian Band Self-Government Act education; social and welfare services; health services; preservation and management of natural resources; preservation, protection and management of fur-bearing animals, fish and game; public order and safety; construction, maintenance and management of roads, operation of businesses, professions and trades et cetera.
In short, the Sechelt people will have a Government accountable to their own electors and not accountable to a remote bureaucracy in Ottawa. They will have a Government determined to use its resources to strengthen that community.
Their type of Government will nurture culture, give life to language and will extend the dimension of this country.
In 1984, the Sechelt people held an historial celebration and placed three carved figures in their community; a young warrior, a mother figure representing culture, and a father figure or headman with a talking stick. But unlike the traditional talking stick, it had no carvings because the Sechelt felt that they lacked achievements under their own authority.
They believe their real identity will come with their understanding of self-government. In the words of the ceremony of that day, they said as a community:
We want to carry our own stick and govern ourselves and be a resource to this great country of ours ... Canada.
I am asking the House, Mr. Speaker, for its best consideration for this Sechelt legislation. I do so for three important reasons. First, it fulfils a dream of the Sechelt people for self-determination and self-government. Second, it represents a first expression of this Government's commitment to a community-based approach to Indian self-government. Third, it is a beginning, a moment in Canadian history to be marked, a time to affirm the Canadian heritage of freedom so clearly intoned in this House on July 1, 1960, by that great parliamentarian, the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker. He said:
I am a Canadian, a free Canadian, free to speak without fear, free to worship God in my own way, free to stand for what I think right, free to oppose what 1 believe wrong, free to choose those who shall govern-
The people of Sechelt want that freedom to be Canadian in a way that respects their history, their culture, their language and their pride in who they are. They want to begin, and they need our help.
That is my appeal to this House for them and for other Indian communities who are working and planning to build their own expression of self-government, which I hope we will have the privilege of considering in the months ahead.
I would normally close now, but before I take my seat, Mr. Speaker, I thought I might conclude my remarks by offering some acknowledgements and thanks to a number of people who worked so very, very hard over the last number of months. Most Bills that come through this House are faceless in the sense that we sometimes fail to recognize the folks who actually do the work.
In this case, the Bill, whatever its advantages, whatever its shortcomings may be seen to be, is the product of some very creative work done by a number of people both in this place and outside of it. I want to make sure they are recognized.
I would like to offer my congratulations and my heartfelt thanks to Chief Stanley Dixon, to his Council and to the people of Sechelt. They exhibited tremendous tenacity, patience and imagination. I want to offer thanks to Mr. Graham Allen, and Mr. Gordon Anderson, advisers to the Sechelt community. I thought of what words to describe their contribution. Tough insistence are the two words which I came up with. I want to thank John Tait, Mary Dawson, Fred Caron and Claude Bisaillon, all from the Department of Justice. They were willing to engage in some imaginative and creative law which can be found in the Bill. Also I want to thank Audrey Doerr of my own Department who pushed, pulled, prodded and pleaded to get it done and bring it home. She was ably assisted by Steve Aronson, Graham Swan and Carol Ann Brewer. I acknowledge the tremendous "beyond the second mile" effort on their part.
Finally, if I could have the indulgence of the House for a moment or two longer, I should like to thank Theresa Nahanee, my legislative assistant, who dreamed and worked and wrote a wee poem which I want to share in my concluding remarks. I received the poem the other day; 1 hope I will not embarrass her. She called it "Sechelt". Theresa Nahanee is not only my legislative assistant; she is a Squamish Indian women from Vancouver. Her poem reads: a giant step for Indian-kind if the arrow is true to its mark -a drop in the ocean if the target be missed (easily corrected) a microcosm of Indian-life to sift through gently to learn from in earnest -the strong, survive the weak, perish in the dustbin of history each minute particle of change represents heroic effort of herculean proportions celebrations of an era -in its time, fought for with vigour in the future, remembered with dignity fling the future to the wind but never to chance for nothing is fixed in man's mind historic changes are marked in light-years, like little sparks flying,
Sparking, dying in their time littering history like a milky way. to the victors, spoils, to the vanquished, defeat for those who struggle, reward for those who don't, nothing opportunities to cast a giant shadow or shed a great light, come not often in a lifetime, but here you have another opportunity, what will it be?
February 7, 1986

What will it mean? history will record.

subtopic: SECHELT INDIAN BAND SELF-GOVERNMENT ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to follow the Minister and to speak on behalf of my Party in respect of what has to be regarded as a most important piece of legislation for the Sechelt Indian people, a piece of legislation for which they have worked and looked forward to for a very long period of time.
When the Minister introduced Bill C-93, it was accompanied by a communique that spoke about a Bill establishing Self-Government for the Sechelt Indian Band. In that communique, the Minister said: "This Act allows the Sechelt Indian Band of British Columbia to move toward Indian self-government".
I would just to indicate, and only in passing, that the word "allows", meaning that the federal Government will permit, will certainly grate upon the ears of some Indian elders in the country who would be very swift, if they had the opportunity at this moment, to remind us that the right to Indian self-government was never at any time in our history relinquished. It was never given up or transferred to any colonial power or to the Government of Canada as we know it today.
The Minister's phrase in the communique, "move toward Indian self-government", perhaps could have been "move further toward Indian self-government". I say that to point out that in fact the Sechelt Indian Band, which consists of 33 reserves and covers some 2,500 acres situated north of Vancouver between Gibson's and Powell River, has already taken advantage of all the optional powers available to it under the Indian Act. In other words, it has occupied all the space which we as a Government allowed them. Of course Hon. Members, and most particular the Minister himself, know that occupying that space is self-government in name only. It is not genuine self-government because under the Indian Act there are still many strings attached, many guidelines and many circulars issued when we allow an Indian band or an Indian Government to take certain over responsibilities.
Nowhere can that be better demonstrated than when we consider how the Government-not just this Government but the previous administration as well-has a different interpretation of Indian control over Indian education. When the document "Indian Control of Indian Education" was first introduced by the then National Indian Brotherhood, it meant exactly what it said, that Indian people were to have full control. It was to be community-based control. But we know that the current administration and the previous one interpreted that as meaning that it was only to allow a degree of participation, which is quite different from Indian control over Indian education.
Be that as it may, I simply point out that the occupying of space under the Indian Act is not Indian self-government. The Sechelt Indian people have occupied that space. They virtually operate all programs and services made available by the Department of Indian Affairs which are appropriate to their
Sechelt Indian Band Self-Government Act
circumstances. For example, the Band has its own primary school. It administers its own social assistance program. It has a housing authority, and it looks after its own economic development. However, let me remind Hon. Members that it is always with provisos, restrictions or limitations. With Bill C-93 the Sechelt band will be able to go further in the direction of self-Government.
This Bill alloows-and again I point out the word "allows"-or devolves power or responsibility from the federal Government, and also some from the provincial administration, but it does not recognize that self-Government is a basic, essential and primary aboriginal right. I will return to that point later in my remarks. Nevertheless, with the passage of Bill C-93, the Sechelt Indian Band will be allowed to become a legal entity. I want to tell my colleagues in the House what that means.
In its own right, the Sechelt Indian Band will have the power to enter into contracts, to hold property, to borrow and to spend money, and even to sue and be sued. At the present time none of those rights can be undertaken by the Band without the consent of the Minister and his officials. Bill C-93 will allow the Sechelt, to a certian extent, to get out from under the totalitarian regime of the Indian Act. Let us be fair and accurate in this regard.
This is not a Bill giving total emancipation to the Sechelt Indian people. It moves toward that and, therefore, my Party and I support it. However, we want it to be seen in its proper context. It moves toward, it allows the Sechelt people, to a certain extent, to get out from under the totalitarian regime imposed upon it by the Indian Act, and out from underneath the paternalism, as well meaning as it often is, of the Minister and his officials. The Sechelt band will be enabled to go on its own to a greater extent than is now possible living under the Indian Act and under the full authority of the Minister. So it will become, first, a legal entity.
Second, Bill C-93 will enable the Sechelt Indian Band to gain legal title to its reserve lands. These lands will be transferred in fee simple to the Band, subject, of course, as I have said before, to certain restrictions. Many Canadian people would be amazed to learn that Indian people do not have legal title to their own reserve lands at the present time. Bill C-93 will change that situation, as the Minister said, with respect to one band which has 2,500 acres of land. There are restrictions, however, but I am not going to dwell on those now. We will examine them more carefully when this Bill is in committee. There are restrictions relating to the ownership and exploitation of minerals, for example.
I want to remind the Minister of the report of the Special Committee on Indian Self-government to which he referred. He indicated that it is now a document that has been accepted by this administration, and for that we express our gratitude. I remind the Minister that the report of the special committee was convinced that in order to ensure that self-government becomes a reality, each Indian First Nation must have full

February 7, 1986
Sechelt Indian Band Self-Government Act rights to control its own lands in the manner that it sees fit. That is somewhat different from what we have in Bill C-93. The legal title to those lands is given, but harken, there are restrictions.
Third, the Band will have its own constitution. It should be noted that the Government must give its approval to any constitution that is adopted by the Band. The Band will have to seek Ottawa's consent for the original constitution, for the approval of that constitution, and later on if there are amendments it must come to Ottawa, to the Governor in Council, to have those amendments approved. That will be of interest to Hon. Members because-

speechtext:
We were at the point where it was indicated that the Sechelt Indian Band will have their own constitution, and how that constitution will come into existence, and how that constitution will be amended. The band will, under its constitution, be able to know what powers it can exercise and what procedures it must follow in the exercise of that self-government. When the Special Committee on Indian Self-government was holding hearings representatives of the Sechelt Indian Band, came before the special committee, and demonstrated that they were progressive and forward-looking in their approach. They did so by presenting to us an example, or a draft of enabling legislation that would permit them to opt out of the Indian Act and operate under a band charter, or constitution, which would have the force of law for that Band.
During those very same hearings we heard also from the Grand Council of the Cree, and they described for us their negotiations with the Government which led eventually to the drafting of the Cree-Naskapi (of Quebec) Act, which has already been enacted into law by the Parliament of Canada. This particular Act was a follow-up, as the Minister said in his speech, to the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement. I want to point out to the House that at the time the Cree appeared before the standing committee to tell us about the negotiations leading to their Act they made it very clear that the legislation they were working toward was, and I quote, "the Cree aspirations and the Cree position".
Chief Stanley Dixon and the council of the Sechelt Band have also stressed that what Bill C-93 does is to meet their urgent needs to be delivered and to be freed from the limitations imposed on them by the powers and the jurisdiction of the Indian Act. I do want to point out, and the Minister has done this as well in his communique, that neither the Cree of northern Quebec, nor the members of the Sechelt Indian Band in British Columbia, have ever suggested for a moment that their particular pieces of legislation are to be regarded in any way as models. Other Indian First Nations are free to accept from either the Cree-Naskapi (of Quebec) Act or from Bill C-93, any appropriate elements. It should be understood that there is no imposition of any kind by this statute upon other Indian First Nations.
I would like to call it one o'clock and continue my remarks after the break.

subtopic: SECHELT INDIAN BAND SELF-GOVERNMENT ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House is debating a Bill introduced by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie), Bill C-93, an Act relating to the establishment of self-government for the Sechelt Indian Band.
I was telling the House earlier that this Band, consisting of some 33 reserves and having 2,500 acres of land, is located in the Province of British Columbia North of Vancouver.
When we recessed at one o'clock I was pointing out, as the Minister did in his remarks, that this is by no means the first time the House has legislated self-government. The previous Parliament legislated the Cree-Naskapi (of Quebec) Act. I think it could be argued quite convincingly that in many ways the Cree-Naskapi (of Quebec) Act was a more progressive piece of legislation. I am not going to take much time of the House to dwell on that. I will leave that to another spokesman for our Party. However, it should be pointed out that the Cree-Naskapi (of Quebec) Act did flow out of what may be described as the bilateral process.
The Cree-Naskapi (of Quebec) Act came out of an agreement that involved Quebec, Canada and the Grand Council of the Cree, the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement. However, the Act itself was negotiated between the federal Government and the Cree and Naskapi people. The Bill we are debating today could be more accurately described as one coming out of a tripartite process. According to this Bill, the British Columbia Government has certain major roles to play.
I will leave it to other spokespersons to point out what part the British Columbia Government will play in the implementation of this legislation. I believe some Hon. Members from British Columbia may wish to dwell on that, and I am sure they will want to express some concerns, because, as we know, in that part of Canada there has not been the most far-sighted understanding of the importance and prominence deserved by the recognition of aboriginal rights. In fact, in that province there has been a very reactionary situation that has led to many sorts of difficulties, the most recent being the case of the Haida people and Lyell Island.
With respect to the Cree-Naskapi (of Quebec) Act, I was emphasizing at one o'clock that the Cree themselves have said that that particular Act represents Cree aspirations and the Cree position. The leaders of the Sechelt Band have expressed the same view but in slightly different words. Chief Stanley Dixon and the Council of the Sechelt Indian Band have stressed that Bill C-93 meets their particular urgent need to be freed to a certain extent, but not entirely from the limitations imposed on them by the Government of Canada. Certainly they will be freed from the jurisdiction imposed upon them by the Indian Act. But as I pointed out earlier, there are still many restrictions imposed on this Band.
When I made those comments, the Minister reacted with some sensitivity, but I think he will have to admit that this is not in any way a Bill of emancipation. It does not in any way provide full self-government, even with respect to the transfer of legal title to the land. We know that there are restrictions of which the British Columbia Government will be very quick to

February 7, 1986
Sechelt Indian Band Self-Government Act
remind the Band, restrictions particularly related to the exploitation of mineral resources.
Neither the Cree-Naskapi (of Quebec) Act nor the Bill regarding the Sechelt Band can be regarded as models for any other Indian First Nation. Never has that been argued, even by the Minister himself. Of course, it can be said that if there are appropriate elements in Bill C-93 or in the Cree-Naskapi (of Quebec) Act that other Indian First Nations may wish to adopt, they are free to do so, but there is to be no imposition of any kind.
The Minister has indicated very clearly that he understands this particular point. In the communique he issued in conjunction with the introduction of the Act he said that this is an example of the community-based approach to self-government reflecting the specific, special or particular circumstances of the Sechelt Band. The Minister strested that it is not a model for other communities. Chief Dixon of the Sechelt Band echoed this very same view when he said that enabling legislation might not be the answer for other Bands and that they will have to choose their own path when they are ready.
I do not want to belabour this point, but again I make the argument that Members of the Flouse who are concerned with policy relating to Indian people are particularly distressed by the situation in British Columbia. None of us should think that Bill C-93 contains any avenues that will help us solve all the difficulties experienced by aboriginal people in the Province of British Columbia. We are not dealing here with a model, and that approach, of course, must always be avoided. I have said, as has the Minister and other Members of Parliament, that there is too much diversity in the Indian community of Canada to have a single model that in any way could Fit the needs or aspirations of all Indian First Nations, and therefore we must avoid imposing that approach. The Special Committee on Indian Self-Government became very much aware of the diversity that exists in Canada when it held its cross-country hearings. That is why in the report we tabled there is no model or description of what self-government should look like. I can remember how disappointed some members of the news media were. They asked us what Indian Self-Government looked like. They felt that there had to be a chart or a graph somewhere. But there was none because none can ever exist. Indigenous self-government must relate to the needs of the people and flow either from traditional sources or from present current needs. Of course, that is what we are doing with the Sechelt Band.
The Sechelt Band legislation is very modern. It meets the needs of these Indian people who are surrounded by other municipalities but cannot act as other municipalities can. They are limited by what we here have imposed upon them by way of the Indian Act and all of the policies and regulations that flow from that Act. It is that from which they are being relieved to a significant extent.
I have to express a little concern. The Deputy Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, when he appeared
before the standing committee, made this observation regarding the Sechelt Indian Bill: "It is not what we consider a model". Good. But then he went on to say: "But rather what we consider an indication as to how far we are willing to go as a department". In other words, what we have here today is the outer limits of how far-if the spokesman from the Department can be believed and that is an accurate reflection of Government policy-the Department will go.

My hon. friend who served on the committee asks how far we can go. That is exactly the point I want to stress. Perhaps it is how far the Department is willing to go or how far it can go, but it is for that very reason that Indian leaders are somewhat apprehensive about the route we are taking today, the so-called legislative path or avenue. That is why Indian leaders continue to stress with vigour that what we have to pursue is the constitutional route. When we have done that, and when we have been successful at the constitutional level, then it will not be how far the Minister or the Department is willing to go or, as my hon. friend opposite said, how far they can go. Rather, it will be what rights or powers flow from the Constitution of Canada. Legislation cannot replace the need for constitutional recognition.
Let us come back to where the Minister took us in his remarks. I have to concur entirely with him when he said that Bill C-93 is a major step forward for the Sechelt Indian Band. That is a fact, that is why I support Bill C-93 and that is why my Party will vote in favour of it. For that Indian Band, this is an historic occasion for which it has planned and worked with great determination and much skill over a very long period of time. But Bill C-93 has to be seen in context. We must return to what I consider to be the touch-stone of the policy of Indian Self-Government, to which the Minister referred, entitled Indian Self-Government in Canada, a Report of the Special Committee.
For the benefit of hon. Members who may not have been here at the time the report was tabled, I will give them the first two recommendations in the report. First, the Committee recommends that the federal Government establish a new relationship with Indian First Nations, and that an essential element of this relationship be recognition of Indian SelfGovernment. What the "new relationship" in this context means is cutting the strings, severing the ties that bind, letting go. I point out to the House that Bill C-93 does not cut all of the strings. It cuts the strings which are in the Indian Act but replaces them with new ones. In fact, it gives the province of British Columbia some strings it didn't have before.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pride and satisfaction that I rise today to comment on this legislation. Before commencing to do so I would like to offer my thanks to the Minister and the Government for bringing the Bill forward. It is an important step. A great many hurdles were overcome. It has been a long process. It has involved more than one Government. Direction has had to be established and the bugs have had to be worked out to bring us to the point we are at today. The Minister and his staff, as well as previous Governments and Parliaments, have worked on this problem and it has now come to a point where I think the Sechelt people are very pleased.
I would also like to extend my thanks to the Official Opposition representative who just spoke. He voiced many important concerns to native people. I know he has supported these people in their endeavours toward self-government and they have a great deal of respect for the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superioe (Mr. Penner), as do many other native people in Canada. The points made by the Hon. Member were certainly not lost today. They will be raised again in committee. The issues which concern him and his Party, as well as ours, will be raised again.
Today is an important day for the Sechelt people in a lot of respects. This Bill is not a product of the current Government alone. It is not a product of the current band administration alone. This is the unfolding of aspirations of the Sechelt people which they have held for many years. There are about 650 people who live on the Sechelt Peninsula in British Columbia. They live in areas which have great potential. Over the years they have felt thwarted in their efforts to use the resources on the lands they occupy in order to bring about a better way of life for their people.
The Indian Act provided an impediment to progress. The Band has been lucky to have had good managers and very active participants in the government of their community. 1 believe the Band has been exemplary in the way in which it has developed. Eventually the Indian Act became a very serious impediment. Alterations were made which allowed Bands discretionary power. Those options were fully utilized by the Sechelt Band. They were able to make the decisions which affected their community in a number of areas. Later those powers became too limited. Progress for native people across the board in Canada did not move forward in a timely manner to aid the people of Sechelt. They began to think in terms of a piece of legislation which would enable them to develop their community resources in a timely way which
Sechelt Indian Band Self-Government Act
would be meaningful to them. I believe that the Band has always had responsible leadership which reflected the wishes of the people. The Bill before us today represents that particular situation.
The interesting thing about this particular legislation is that it goes back at least 10 years. Many people have been responsible for bringing it forward. I want to give credit, on the record, to the people who have been involved with it. They include Chief Stan Dixon and the present Council of the Sechelt Indian Band, Benedict Pierre, Clarence Joe, Lloyd Jefferies, Ann Quinn, Gilbert Joe, former Chief Calvin Crai-gan, and Ted Dixon, a very well respected member of that community who was active in bringing forward the concerns of the Sechelt people on this and other issues. There was a very strong force which assisted the people of Sechelt to bring this, as well as many other projects, forward. Involved in developing this concept, filling out the framework, doing the detailed work, and providing an enormous amount of the energy which brought it forward, were the Band's legal adviser, Graham Allen, and the Band's financial adviser, Gordon Anderson.
There have been years of blood, sweat, tears and enormous frustration and problems. Instead of yielding to those frustrations they reorganized, applied more effort and more resources, and overcame the impediments. They convinced people that their course of action was correct and needed to be heeded and dealt with. We have the ultimate product of that before us today.
Mention has been made of the provincial Government in British Columbia. There are certainly occasions on which we disagree with it. It is interesting to note that the provincial Government does appear to support the thrust and direction of this legislation. It would appear that it is prepared to make moves to complement the Sechelt Indian Band Act and bring the desires of the Sechelt Indian people to fruition. We support that. I think the Government of British Columbia will make an effort to co-operate with this legislation.
On the other side of the coin, the Member for Cochrane-Superior has alluded to the problems in other areas with native people. The Government does seem to have a course of action which is not conductive to co-operation with some Indian bands. Ultimately, as is the way in our country, the people of British Columbia will make the decisions on those issues.
I would like to conclude my remarks by again thanking the Minister and the representative of the official Opposition, the Member for Cochrane-Superior, for assisting in bringing forth an agreement today which will allow this Bill to pass through the House. We will definitely hear more about this in committee. subtopic: PENSION BENEFITS STANDARDS ACT, 1985 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will speak very briefly because I believe there is consent by all Parties to move this legislation forward as well. It has been 10 years since the subject of pension reform was first raised in the country. There have been 10 years of study, and now is the time for action. I have participated in the debate for most of those 10 years.
It is interesting to trace how many levels of Government have studied the problem. The Quebec Government has studied the issue with the Cofirentes Plus. The Ontario Royal Commission has studied it. The Lazar Interdepartmental Task Force has studied it at the federal Government level, as has the Senate Task Force on Aging. We have had the National Pension Conference, which I was privileged to be able to announce in the House on behalf of the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) nearly seven years ago. There was the Ontario Select Committee on Pension Reform, as well as the House of Commons Task Force on Pension Reform chaired by the Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith).
This Bill and those which will follow it are among the most important social measures that this House will examine in this session, because they deal with the issue of poverty among the elderly and the prevention of poverty among the future elderly. This Bill contains many specific provisions which will improve the situation of the elderly in the future. We are guaranteeing access to pensions for part-time workers. We are improving vesting, introducing, for the first time, portability provisions, providing for disclosure to employees and employee representatives of the state of the fund and of benefits accrued, looking after widows and widowers by making survivors' pensions mandatory, and looking after women by ensuring that they receive benefits equal to those received by men from pension funds. We are improving death benefits out of pension funds on a mandatory basis.
I am pleased, as I am sure are Members of all Parties, that the pension critics for the Liberal and New Democratic Parties
support this Bill. They raised three issues in their speeches on the Bill which I would like to deal with. The first issue raised by both Members was that of the CPP changes which are part and parcel of the reforms recommended by the House of Commons Task Force on Pensions. In particular, the Member for Sudbury argued that we should be bringing homemakers' pensions forward on a rapid basis. That is outside the scope of this particular Bill, but the Government agrees with him and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has indicated in the House that we intend to proceed with that measure as quickly as possible. We hope to have that measure in place by January 1, 1987. I hope that the Member for Sudbury will use his considerable influence on the new Government of Ontario to ensure that it feels as strongly as he does so that we can bring this forward on January 1, 1987. That is something which will dramatically reduce poverty among our elderly. As he is aware, I testified in favour of this at his committee when I was representing the Canadian Institute of Actuaries. Indeed, I was involved in bringing that measure forward to the Progressive Conservative convention when it was adopted as part of our Party policy.
The second issue raised by the Member is that the pension task force recommended that we should implement inflation indexing for pensions. Again, I agree with the Hon. Member for Sudbury and, as he is aware, I testified before his committee on behalf of the Canadian Institute of Actuaries, not only indicating that it was desirable but also how we could do it.
The Hon. Member is very thorough and has read the Bill. I am sure he is aware that Clause 21(5) of the Bill makes provision for outlining what types of inflation protection will receive credit by the federal Government in recognition of the obligations that employers undertake.
Although we were unable to carry the provinces with us, we hope that the introduction of this clause will encourage the private sector to bring in these inflation protection measures on a sound financial basis and indeed encourage other provinces to buy into this procedure in order to make pension reform work.
When the committee studies this Bill, we will table papers showing how we chose the formula in Clause 21(5), and how employers can introduce sound indexing and inflation protection on a basis which does not expose them to unlimited cost. We will be in a position to explain why this basis was chosen, and I hope the Hon. Member for Sudbury uses his considerable influence to persuade the Ontario Government to replicate the provisions in our Bill. As he knows, that Government backed away from inflation protection and I hope it will recognize that we are taking a positive step forward.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, can the Member tell us why this legislation does not include a provision so that surpluses which may accrue in a pension fund can be pumped back into the fund for the benefit of the employees rather than simply taken over by the employer investor?

subtopic: PENSION BENEFITS STANDARDS ACT, 1985 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I raised this issue in my opening remarks. When the provincial consensus was being developed, there were no examples before us of the type of situation which had developed with the Dominion Store workers within the last few months. Almost without exception, employers had acted responsibly. When they had made surplus withdrawals, it had been to get money to keep the company alive. Many companies, and I am sure the Member is aware of them particularly in the transport sector back in the 1981-82 period, needed access to funds just to stay alive. The particular provision in this Bill says that the companies can have access to funds where that access does not impair the solvency of the fund. Companies cannot get any more back except that which was surplus to the obligations they committed to.
Since the time this Bill was tabled it has become apparent, and I think there is a well known high profile case I cited in my speech, and no doubt the Member will cite it in hers- where it is felt there may well be injustices to workers. The fact that there had not been a problem up to that time is the main reason that there is nothing in the Bill to prohibit it.
February 7, 1986

In the United States, which brought in a similar provision prohibiting entirely withdrawals of surpluses, there has been ample demonstration that that type of approach to the problem is counter-productive. It is counter-productive because employers stopped funding on anything other than the minimum basis. They left the minimum amount of assets in the fund, and when they got into Financial difficulty the funds folded and the workers were left high and dry.
If you bring in a strict prohibition against withdrawal of surpluses, as we can see now from nearly seven years of experience in the United States, the effect is to leave workers in a worse off position. Employers take steps to reduce their contributions to the bare minimum in order not to get caught. It is not as simple as just prohibiting the withdrawal of surpluses and saying that means workers will be better off.
We have all kinds of evidence. The pension benefit guarantee fund in the United States has lost hundreds of millions of dollars as a result of the actions that employers have taken by minimizing funding and then leaving the fund high and dry when employers got into trouble.
Mir. Deputy Speaker: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps).

subtopic: PENSION BENEFITS STANDARDS ACT, 1985 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join in this debate because the Hon. Member who spoke to the Government's position on the proposed pension legislation has made a number of assertions, assertions that somehow this legislation would be of great benefit to those among our society who currently represent the poor, in particular women, and those women in poverty.
This piece of legislation does include a shorter vesting period. Obviously we in the Liberal Party support that because the Liberal Party in the budget of Marc Lalonde originally introduced the notion of reducing the vesting period. Our Party supports more portability in pensions. Our Party supports a reduced vesting period to allow the kind of pension mobility that we know is following the mobility of workers in society. It is important we have this portability so workers can feel if they move from job to job, as is currently the case in a highly mobile Canadian society, that those workers will continue to have coverage. However, the Government's position and refusal to look at the issue of full indexation in fact belie and contradict the very claims made by the Hon. Member in respect of the leadership of the federal Government on this issue.
We know that under the previous Liberal Government the national policy was committed to a full indexation of pension plans. Now we hear Government spokesmen saying that they would rather leave it to the private sector, somehow hoping that private companies will take their responsibility and in fact provide a clause for full inflation protection. That has not been the case in the past. The Government continues to support a pension fund where the excess of the investment can be withdrawn by the company for use in developing its profits
Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985
margins, supplying other products and expanding into new areas. Essentially this is not for the benefit of those who contributed to the pension plan, but for the benefit of shareholders of the company. There is a principle involved here which speaks to whose dollars are in the pension fund. Are they dollars for the shareholders? Are they dollars for company products? Are they dollars for workers who have contributed with matching contributions from companies to provide their own future inflation protection and retirement benefits? I suggest that we are speaking about the latter. Those pension funds should be solely directed toward the payment of pension benefits to retiring and outgoing workers. The company should not be permitted to skim off the cream of pension investments. Otherwise, the pension fund is not being used for the benefit of workers and the investment is not there to assist in the retirement of workers but is there to pass off an extra few cents or dollars to the shareholders, to the management of the company or to the company's bottom line.
Why does this particular measure discriminate against the majority of employees who work for small businesses in Canada? When I speak of small businesses, I am talking about businesses with less than 50 employees. Many of the provisions, including the establishment of a pension committee and an invitation to have some worker involvement in the investment process of the company, are restricted to those companies with 50 or more employees. If we are truly concerned about the tripartite approach of labour, management and Government which we as a Parliament have paraded over the last number of years, both previous Liberal Governments and the current Conservative Government, then we should encourage worker involvement in pension funds at the company level, even if the workers happen to work for a company with less than 50 employees. We should not only encourage that type of involvement, but we should facilitate it by suggesting that any worker in any organization where workers want some involvement in the kinds of investments which will be used to guarantee their future retirement should be permitted to do so. In light of current Government changes, as they specifically relate to the Government's consideration of pension benefits as income for the purposes of calculating unemployment insurance, we will see that more and more workers will want a direct say in what happens in their company pension plans.
At the same time as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is introducing the Pension Benefits Standards Act and subsequent Conservative Members are speaking to it, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) is creating a disincentive to private pension plans by introducing the new notion that, for unemployment insurance, pension benefits will now be considered as income. That has created a two-class system of citizens. The first class includes those citizens who are not salaried employees. Not only does this particular measure indicate that those with pension benefits will not be allowed to collect unemployment insurance, it applies only to those who are salaried employees with a company pension plan. However, if one happens to be in business and has contributed to a private money purchase plan, an RRSP, the

February 7, 1986
Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985 Minister of Employment and Immigration has said in her wisdom that one is exempt from the new regulations. In other words, an upper-middle income Canadian, who has had an opportunity to contribute to a private Registered Retirement Savings Plan, which has accrued and built up over the years, and has retired from work, will be entitled to collect unemployment insurance benefits for the 52 weeks following retirement if he or she has not yet reached the age of 65 years. At the same time, salaried employees who are in company pension plans are denied that right.
When we adopted the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, we said that all citizens and residents of Canada were created equal, with the same rights and obligations. It is not only this particular pension measure which discriminates against employees of companies with less than 50 workers. A concurrent measure of another Minister dealing with pension benefits indicates that salaried employees, such as steelworkers in the riding of Hamilton East, will not be allowed to collect unemployment insurance as long as they are receiving a pension from their companies. At the same time, if I am forced into retirement by the voters of Hamilton East and have an RRSP-and subsequently I can take another job or cash in my RRSP-I can collect unemployment. Is it more important for the steelworker in the riding of Hamilton East, the salaried employee or company person, to collect a pension or is it more important for the upper middle-income Canadian who has contributed to a private money purchase plan to be able to collect unemployment insurance?
We have been elected to protect those who are least able to protect themselves. Those of us who can afford private money purchase plans, who can afford to play the stock-market and who can afford accountants to give us the loopholes we need so that we do not have to pay as much in taxes as we might have to do if we were straight salaried employees, have built in protection. It is the salaried company person who does not even have any input into how his or her pension funds are spent who is hamstrung by the decision of the Government. If in fact good pension investments should result in a higher than average yield and in an increase over what was expected for the pension plan, such workers, unlike private RRSP investors, will not be able to take advantage of that excess. That excess can be skimmed by the company and sunk back into its profit margins, its president's salary and its shareholders' return. The people who will be left holding the bag will be those who thought they had a greater say in pension funds as a result of the mesures about which we are talking today.
Many issues have not been addressed in this particular Bill. They have actually been ignored. The difficulties have been compounded by the current position taken by the Government in respect of the calculation of pension benefits as earnings for the purpose of unemployment insurance.
When the Hon. Member commented upon the situation facing the women of the country, he neglected to say that while the particular Act will obviously be of benefit to those people who are currently in a pension plan or are currently in a company with over 50 employees, it does nothing to speak to
the basic inequities currently being faced by senior citizens and elderly women between 55 and 65 years of age who may find themselves, through no fault of their own, never having been in a company pension plan.

Mr. Speaker, this Government which is talking about equity for women and the poor, which has just announced a program under the Bill for women or widows between the ages of 60 and 65, this Government is at the same time discriminating against women who have never married or who for whatever reason are divorced or separated. In other words, the Government Member would have us believe the Government is doing its best for women who have no other means of support. However, we all know that under the Bill announced in 1985 by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, which concerns women between the ages of 60 and 65, these women were not covered if they were single or divorced. They were not entitled to the same pensions offered to widows, a group the Government had decided to give a pension.
So there are some very large gaps, not just in this Bill but in the Government's whole policy on pensions.
Speaking of the Bill, I think it has two major shortcomings, one being the Government's decision to reject the policy of the previous Liberal Government by saying that every pension plan must contain guarantees against inflation.
Mr. Speaker, we now know, whatever may be said from time to time in this House by our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), that the real rate of inflation in 1986 is practically the highest ever. For instance, the banks are offering us from 6 to 7 per cent on our investments, while they are charging from 11.5 up to as much as 14 per cent on mortgages and other types of loans.
So, the so-called spread between the real rate and the rate charged by the banks is 6 or 7 per cent, which is much higher than what we had two or three years ago.
When we see the spread between the interest rates and the rates charged by the banks, we have to conclude that the Government has ignored the pleas of Canadians, of employees and companies, for real protection against inflation, while we also know that the real rate of inflation continues to widen the gaps.
I would say that especially the elderly and those living on pensions are among those who are least protected against inflation. We young people who are in good health can always go out to work or find another job, or even have two jobs or find some other way to save money. When we look at a person who has to take early retirement at 60 for health reasons, that person does not have the same ability to adjust to inflation rates of 6 per cent, 7 per cent, 8 per cent, 10 per cent, 11 per cent, 12 per cent and 13 per cent, as is happening at the present time.
February 7, 1986

1 think it is much more important for the Government, first of all, to provide protection against inflation, and second, this would have been a very good Bill if the Government had decided that the funds invested in these pension plans... If the investment happens to be a good one and the pension fund has a surplus over what it is supposed to have, I think this would have been a good piece of legislation if the Government had decided to give employees the right to return these funds to the pension plan.
Mr. Speaker, what is happening now is that if we end up with a surplus in the pension fund, we allow the companies and employers the possibility to use these surpluses either as profits or to return them to the investors, without really giving employees the opportunity to benefit themselves from the surpluses in their pension funds.
What is the purpose of a pension fund, Mr. Speaker? It's not intended for the investors, for the company or to make profits. The pension fund is there to help employees when they retire. That is the reason why we are dealing with this Bill today. That is the reason why the federal Government has decided to act in a responsible manner and to create a climate where uniform pension funds can be developed.
But when the Government refuses to allow these pension funds to be re-invested for the benefit of the employees, it shows it is more interested in protecting the interests of companies than those of the workers who, in all fairness, should have the opportunity to benefit from surpluses which result from their own investments in the company.
We see, Mr. Speaker, that because of these two shortcomings the Government has failed to recognize the importance of employee involvement and employee contribution to private company pension plans by refusing to provide full inflation protection and by refusing to allow surpluses that may occur in pension funds to be pumped back into the employee's pension benefits. The federal Government is saying that, in fact, it does not really believe that employees, first and foremost, should be involved in the management of their company pension plans. Employees should not have that opportunity except if, by some happenstance, they are employed by a company of 50 or more people and if, by some happenstance, the company happens to have agreed to some type of inflation protection. It is the same kind of voluntary approach of the private sector that we see has failed so dismally when it comes to the so-called Challenge '85 and Challenge '86 programs.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration said: "Leave it to the private sector, they are going to create jobs. Leave it to the private sector, they are going to give us inflation protection". I dare say that the workers in the steelmills in Hamilton know they have been able to accrue some inflation protection by the sweat of their brows and not because of any largess on the part of a company boss. In fact, some of those workers have gone on strike, some of them have been forced to walk a picket line to get the kind of inflation protection that is
Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985 now built into their pension plans. In the same breath we see that that inflation protection, that particular benefit-if you want to consider it so, a carrot that might encourage people to take early retirement-has not only been ignored by the lack of inflation protection in this particular Bill, but has been further jeopardized because of the action of the Minister of Employment and Immigration when she told the workers and the salaried employees of this country: "You will no longer be eligible for unemployment insurance because you are on a pension plan".
Mr. Speaker, if you were a union negotiator and you were negotiating a contract which would be coming up for renewal in 1986, would you tell your older workers that they should be looking for more pension contributions? Would you tell your older workers that the company should be building up the pension funds and encouraging early retirement to allow younger employees to come on to the job? No, you would tell them to get the bottom line now, get into private RRSPs and get out of the pension company system, because the Minister of Employment and Immigration has introduced discriminatory legislation.
