speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have a chance to say a few words on the matter of the Government's pension reform Bill. I would like to introduce what I am saying with a few comments on what I see as the background of the principle of pensions.
Private pensions are something that only a minority of the workers of Canada enjoy because most pension plans have been negotiated by unions with their employers and it is only a minority of the workers who have as yet attained union status. Therefore, pensions are always negotiated as part of the wage package. There are the official wages and there are other economic benefits in the contract, and then there are pensions, if there are pensions. Of course, by no means have all unions been able to negotiate pensions as yet.
I recall that for 12 years as an officer in my local union, I was helping to develop the pension policies of our company, Continental Can. The company did have a pension plan. We had to negotiate improvements to it. Every time we negotiated a new contract every one or two years, the company said that there is this much in the pension fund and that much in wages, or we could have it all in wages or we could have it all in the pension plan. There were different ways the package would be
offered, but the money in the pension plan was traded off against our wages. It is a very important principle that at least half of the money in the pension fund is the workers' money. The other half of it that the company puts in in the formal sense is also there by virtue of negotiations. It is part of the package that the workers negotiate. It is traded off against wages, against hours, against working conditions and fundamentally it is part of what is traded off for the goodwill and co-operation of the workers and the no-strike clause in the contract that lasts for the length of the contract. That point is not sufficiently recognized by many employers. Notorious for this is Conrad Black who took millions of dollars out of a pension fund because he felt he had a legal loophole which enabled him to do so. However, what he did was thoroughly immoral. Morally speaking, it was theft. He took money that belonged to the workers to use for his own private purposes without any moral excuse whatsoever. This Bill only goes a very small distance toward recognizing that principle.
Our Party will be supporting the Bill because it represents a small progress, but it falls far short of what would be just, and in fact it falls far short of what the Government promised. The main object of the Bill is to regulate the private pension funds of the country. It does not apply to the federal public servants who are already governed under the Public Service Superannuation Act. The Government says that it will extend comparable benefits to those employees, but of course it has not said when it will do so. Why the Government did not bring that forward at the same time as this Bill is something it has not told us. We are being asked to believe that the Government will do it reasonably soon and in reasonable conformity with its promises.
Although we are supporting this Bill because of its degree of progress, we have to object to, and hope there will be some improvement in, two particular faults of this Bill. One fault which has already been mentioned is the fact that it does not provide mandatory inflation protection. It does not protect the workers against having a pension that may have looked good at the time it was negotiated but may be peanuts by the time the workers have retired and are collecting on it. The Bill also notoriously fails to provide any protection against the kind of theft that Conrad Black practised against the workers of Dominion Stores. Why the Government refuses to protect against that, of course, is something that it has not told us.
In an inflationary situation, the workers get hit twice. They get hit once because retired workers find their pensions are worth much less than they thought they would be and much less than they were led to expect they would be. It hurts future pension beneficiaries because it encourages the employer, as in the Conrad Black case, to look at the surplus in the pension fund which has grown because of inflation and to decide to scoop it out rather than convert it back into benefits for the employees who paid for it and earned it.
We very much hope that in committee, Government Members will see fit to agree to amend this Bill in those two respects. At least, we hope they would honour the promise that was made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his
February 7, 1986

Budget and to honour the Government policy statement, Better Pensions for Canadians, which was issued in 1982 by the previous Government and which many workers took as being a guideline for what the Government might do.
Two things are needed to bring minimal justice to this Bill rather than the half-justice for which we will have to vote if the Government refuses to relent. The first thing needed for minimal justice in this Bill is the provision of mandatory protection against inflation, not voluntary protection. I do not know of employers or vendors who have been willing voluntarily to give a break to their workers or consumers as against inflation. It has to be made mandatory, either through Government legislation or through union action. Union action may very well have to include strike action.
Workers may be forced once again to go on strike to get decent pensions for themselves, for those who have retired and for those who may come after them. Many Members on the opposite side deplore strikes and wish that unions would not use their only weapon, the strike. It would be sensible for those Hon. Members to amend this legislation in such a way that public opinion, which recognizes the need for pensions and the need that workers' money in these pensions should be used to their benefit, should find expression in legislation by this Government, by this Parliament, which would ensure that the pension funds are protected against inflation and that they are protected against theft by the employer.
There is, of course, a better way to do this. There is a better way still which our Party has advocated and which our predecessor Party, the CCF, advocated and which those who founded the CCF were advocating even before the CCF was founded, that is, a Government pension such as the Canada and Quebec pension. That would be the most just and economical way of ensuring a decent level of retirement income for all Canadians. But to do that, the rate of benefit of the Canada and Quebec pension would have to be sharply increased. Those workers who can negotiate with their employers, those minority workers who are in the fortunate position of being in unions and able to negotiate with their employers for a private pension, which will be in addition to their Canada and Quebec pension, of course, at the present time find that they are obliged to do that as a matter of prudence because they have no reason to believe that this Government will increase the Quebec and Canada pension to a level that provides for a decent living. But if this Government, on the one hand, wished to avoid strikes, by those workers in a position to struggle for better pensions, or if it wished, on the other hand, to avoid the compulsory, that is the mandatory, inflation protection we are asking for, the Government has a simple solution. It could announce that it will increase the Canada Quebec Pension Plan to a level that makes it unnecessary for workers to negotiate away part of their wages in return for a private pension plan.
The Government has two good options if it does not wish to promote industrial unrest, that is, either make a suitable
Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985
increase in the Canada Quebec Pension Plan or else amend this legislation by including genuine mandatory inflation protection and ensure protection against the employer lifting the surplus out of the pension fund.
I hope that suggestion will be taken quite seriously by the Government Members.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to comment briefly on Bill C-90 to make changes to the pension plans of companies and organizations under the jurisdiction of the Government of Canada.
We Find that this timely piece of legislation includes several measures which will be of great benefit to people who work for the Canadian Government or for companies under its jurisdiction.
Indeed the Bill takes into consideration the fact that the situation has changed drastically over the years. It will make it a lot easier to administer pension plans and give more leeway to individuals who will now be able to transfer their pension funds from one employer to another, an option which workers have now been seeking for several decades.
We want to see this Bill get second reading and be referred to committee, but it does not necessarily mean that we fully endorse all its provisions. For instance, we are anxious to send the Bill to a committee of the House for further consideration because we know that several groups have already expressed the wish to appear as witnesses in an attempt to amend some of the clauses of the Bill. Indeed, one of the changes on which the workers will certainly insist relates to the indexation of their pension benefits. In other words, they want those benefits protected against erosion due to increases in the consumer price index.
Unfortunately that is probably the most obvious shortcoming of this measure-it offers no protection whatsoever against inflation. Hon. Members who have been in the House for some time will recall some of the proposals made in the past. For instance, when the Hon. Marc Lalonde was Minister in the previous Government he proposed a formula which I will outline in a few moments. From the outset, Mr. Speaker, I can say I did not think it was overly generous, but at least the formula did take into account the fact that a worker's pension is regularly eroded by the ever rising cost of living. Mr. Lalonde's formula was simple enough: take the increase in the consumer price index, deduct 2.5 per cent from this and then grant 60 per cent of that Figure as an hedge against inflation. If the inflation rate were about 5 per cent, for instance, we would take away 2.5 per cent, which would leave 2.5 per cent, and pay 60 per cent of that amount, which would mean that,

February 7, 1986
Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985 in a period when the consumer price index goes up by 5 per cent, pensioners would receive a protection of only 1.5 per cent. That is not a lot. However, it would at least be somewhat more than a symbolical recognition of the fact that pensions are eroded by inflation, and I am quite surprised that this Government has not introduced such a minimal protection because it really is the least that we could do, and I am sure that many employees of companies covered by this legislation would not be satisfied with it. I have to ask myself why the proposals of the Government do not take into account the negative effects of inflation on the amount of pensions. When this legislation is referred to a committee, as it will be before long, it will be very important to think seriously about amending it to provide more than a symbolical protection for pensions so that they will not be constantly eroded by inflation.
Another part of the legislation which seems seriously defective is the description of part-time workers. As we know, in well-managed pension plans, full-time workers make contributions to the plan, or at least such is the case in most civilized societies. There are also companies where part-time workers have the option of contributing to the pension plan. However, I find the description of part-time worker contained in this legislation insufficient and defective. The Bill says that, to be a part-time worker, someone must have accumulated over one year 35 per cent of normal annual earnings, which means that he must have worked about one-third of the time, which seems reasonable at first glance. However, according to our research, if this standard is applied, there will probably not be more than 20 per cent of part-time workers eligible, especially in the case of women. And this for the obvious reason that there are more women than men employed in temporary jobs, part-time jobs in our Canadian society. It is more normal for a female employee to spend certain parts of her time at home, and certain times at work. According to our estimate, if we were to apply that 35-per-cent standard to maximum annual earnings, we would find ourselves in the situation where there might be four women out of five who might not have the opportunity to participate in a pension plan. This in our view is an aspect the Government should be considering and assessing before the legislation is passed.
Also, concerning protection against inflation, both in the definition or description of part-time work, it is our firm intention, when the legislation goes before the appropriate committee of the House of Commons, to suggest changes and to move amendments. I hope that at that point, after the debate in this House, the Government will agree to give particular attention to those two areas and make the changes that are needed in my view.
This being said, Mr. Speaker, we have no intention of protracting the debate on Bill C-90, but only to take the time needed to make the Government realize, before we go to committee, that it is most important that some of the shortcomings I have just described should be corrected before the
Bill is returned to the House at report stage so we will have before us, at the end of our discussions at the report stage and third reading, a bill that will be closer to perfection than this one. Those, Mr. Speaker, were the comments I wanted to bring to the attention of the House and the Government at this stage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make a few comments about these amendments which have been so long in gestation that there must be people who have retired and died since they were originally proposed back in the 1960s. It is scandalous that so many pension plans seem to be designed to benefit not the employee but only the employer. They give the illusion of protection but it is not followed through. The rules for vesting are so inappropriate because they require that an employee attain the age of 45 and have more than 10 years of service before benefits can be vested. That is being changed in this Bill and it is a welcome change. However, it has taken a heck of a long time to get to that point. I believe the reason for that is that the employers and the pension industry have not wanted those changes to be made. I want to go on record as condemning their record and their failure to understand the necessity of providing income security for that large number of people who work for employers where there are pension plans regulated under federal or provincial legislation.
When I was in the Ontario Legislature the question of pension reform came up frequently. We had a royal commission. It was studied by a legislative committee. Vast amounts of studies and research were produced. However, what we could not get around was the lack of political will by the Conservative Government of Ontario and the then Liberal Government of Canada to make the necessary moves. The only place where reform really came forward was in the Province of Manitoba under an NDP Government. That province decided, regardless of the failure of other provinces and the federal Government to move, that they would make the necessary and desirable reforms in order to ensure that employees who contributed to pension plans had a good chance of actually benefiting from them.
We finally have some changes. They are watered down and inadequate. In particular, they are objectionable because they only apply after 1987. They do not take into account contributions people have made prior to the beginning of next year. Some might say it is better to have that than to have nothing. We say that too. The NDP is supporting this Bill. We discussed it in caucus and decided that although we object to the failure to back-date and the fact it falls short of what is needed, we had better support the Bill because it is the best we are going to get from this Government. It is a heck of a lot better as well than what we got from the previous Government when nothing was done on this subject at all. Nonetheless, let us not fool ourselves. There are still an awful lot of loopholes in the Bill which will allow our pension legislation to continue
February 7, 1986

benefiting employers to the disadvantage of employees who have a legitimate need of income security through the contributions they make.
The fundamental problem here is that there is a real quarrel out there as to just who pension contributions belong to and whether or not they are a form of deferred income. It has been increasingly accepted that they are a form of deferred income. If an employer contributes 7 per cent or 8 per cent of an employee's wages or salary to a pension fund, then as far as I am concerned that money should be seen as belonging to the employee and be used for his or her benefit. That should be a fundamental principle. These days it is becoming more and more obvious that long-term employment in one particular job will become less and less the norm. That is happening now and I suppose there are many Members of this House who have already had two, three or four different careers. Perhaps they were in business, perhaps they were teachers. Perhaps they began in a trade or they went on to take post-graduate studies or practise law. I was a journalist, an alderman, a provincial MPP and now I am a federal MP. I might be a business consultant some day trying to wake up the business community to the needs of working people.

Who knows? I am the only socialist MBA in this House, with the exception of my friend from Kenora-Rai-ny River who shares that distinction with me. Perhaps there are one or two back-benchers in the Conservative Party who have not revealed their true stripes.
We still have a long way to go before the principle that contributions made by employers as well as employees rightly belong to the employee is universal. I am glad to see that harmonized legislation is now coming forward from the provinces and the federal Government to implement Bill C-90. However, that is not going nearly far enough. Other elements of income security which are important have not yet been into place. In fact, the Government is actively leading the way in the opposite direction. Today I was preparing a brief to the Forget Commission on unemployment insurance. One of the points I want to make is that the Government's decision to disallow unemployment insurance benefits for any person receiving more than a certain amount of pension income prior to the age of 65 is a fundamentally objectionable principle. It will hurt ex-service people and Public Service employees who retire before 65. It will also hurt people in the private sector who chose early retirement or are compelled to take early retirement at a reduced rate. They are then looking for some form of income security from a job, but if they lose it they will have no right to unemployment insurance benefits in return for the premiums they will be compelled to pay. The Quebec Pension Plan allows for retirement before 65. The pension is less than the full rate, but the right exists and that has not yet been put into the CPP. Obviously it should be included in order to correspond with the right of early retirement provided for under federal jurisdiction in this Bill. The QPP provides for an increased rate of pension benefits to people who chose to
Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985 retire after the age of 65, and that is a flexibility we should see in our pension arrangements in this Bill as well as the CPP.
My colleagues have talked about specific measures in the Bill. This Bill does not apply to federal public servants and they are now being compelled to accept a situation where the indexation they have fought for is going to be taken away. It does not cover people in the Forces who have very serious problems and who are being given absolutely no say in the management of a pension fund which amounts to some $13 billion. This is nominally in their account but they have not say at all in its management. As my colleagues have said, this Bill does not ensure that all retirees will enjoy adequate, dignified retirement incomes. It only covers a proportion of people under federal jurisdiction who happen to have pension plans.
I do want to talk about those persons because, if we can get decent standards for them, they will not be in the position of requiring the guaranteed income supplement or other forms of assistance from the federal or other Treasuries after they retire. They will be able to live in dignity. They will be able to be sun-seekers, if they want, or to live in the country with dignity. They will not be under the constraints which govern people who live out their retirements in poverty today.
There are some fundamental principles which must be considered. The first is that the net effect of this Bill is very negligible for the next few years because vesting after two years is only provided for with respect to contributions after 1987. There are large numbers of employees under the age of 45 who work in federally-regulated jurisdictions who now have up to 15 or 20 years of service with an employer and who still stand at risk of losing the benefit of the employer's contributions and the benefit of vesting in the foreseeable future. That could continue for as long as 10 or 15 years with respect to persons who may have 10 years of service and are aged 30. They will not reach the magic age of 45 for some time, and they have no right to the employer's contribution for the years of service they have now.
There could have been some negotiation on that front. It could have been provided that the full rate of interest on employers' contributions would not begin to be paid until after this Bill was proclaimed. It seems to me that the Bill should now be amended to provide that when employees have been in a particular job for a number of years they should not lose the benefit of vesting if they should happen to lose or change their job prior to reaching the age of 45 and meeting the requirements under the previous Pension Benefits Act. That is very objectionable, Mr. Speaker.
I think the two-year rule is too long. It should probably be only one year, at least for anyone over the age of 25, at which time the work careers of people begin to settle down. To forward date it means that it will be a long time before people who are contemplating retirement now will be assured of substantial portability in their pension benefits. This Bill does not provide for instant portability, despite what the pension
10604

February 7, 1986
Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985 industry and private employers want to tell us. It provides for a very qualified amount of portability. The first portability provided for under this Bill, believe it or not, will not occur for about 1,000 days, that is not until January 1, 1989.
I welcome the fact that the Bill provides for making information available to employees. However, some improvements could be made in those particular provisions. The actuarial and other information should be on file at the administrator's office and should be available to plan members and their unions at any time. However, I do welcome the fact that that information will be available. I hope we do not get into silly situations whereby employees who seek to look at that information are denied the right to take copies or to make copies at a reasonable charge.
The provisions for the direction of the plans are quite unacceptable as far as I am concerned. I do not care how much protestation there is from employers about this. I find the idea that employers shall continue to be the sole administrators of pension funds objectionable and unacceptable.
I have given a great deal of thought to the question of how the Canadian industry should work in the future. Everything that I see and hear, not only from my friends in the trade union movement, but also from business consultants, from the example of Japan, and from management consultants in the United States, indicates that if we in North America are going to be competitive in a very difficult world environment over the course of the next years, we will have to build relationships built on trust and co-operation in the workplace rather than on the current practice which seems to prevail whereby the employer knows best and tries to treat the employees like dirt.
That means that pensions should be run on a joint basis by employers and employees with equal representation on the board directing the administrator, possibly with a neutral chairman. That kind of arrangement could and should have been included in this particular Bill. The current provisions give employees no guarantee of any say in the administration of pension funds if there are fewer than 50 employees. Most people who study the subject know that it is very difficult for employees to get together and say that they want to exercise their rights because they do not have an organized mechanism by which they can make the provisions stick.
In addition, this Bill says that there will be only a consultative committee and that employees will have the right to representation on some unexplained basis, direct or indirect, on that consultative committee. The committee could have 10 or 15 members and there would only be a requirement that one be representative of the employee. There is no guarantee that the committee will give any credence or voice to the objections or concerns which may be raised by the employee representative. There is no guarantee that the employee representative will not be that of the middle management employees covered by a particular plan. The blue collar, pink collar, or white collar employee may have no representation at all. I think that is inadequate and the Government should have recognized that in drafting the Bill. It should recognize that now and bring
forward appropriate amendments to that particular part of the Bill.
I believe the employees should have a substantial voice in the policies and investment provisions of the pension fund in which an important part of their future security is put. On the one hand, I think that is more effective than only having investment rules that are administered by a superintendent of insurance or of pension schemes here in Ottawa. Second, I think it lends itself to innovative forms of finance into which many employees may be prepared to have their pension fund enter.
What happens, for example, if a particular enterprise which has $10 million or $15 million in its pension fund is in a difficult situation? It may well be that employees under that situation would be prepared to see up to 25 per cent of the value of their pension fund used in a rescue effort to get that company back on the rails. That is a possibility. It may well be that a pension fund could be used to provide important benefits to employees. Many employees cannot currently afford to make an investment in a house. Yet, at the same time, they may have credits in a pension fund which, if they could draw on them, would permit them to make such an investment.
I am not sure whether there has been agreement among the House Leaders that this matter should come to a vote now. I understand that some of my colleagues may have some comments to make. If not, I am sure the matter could come to a vote later. I know that the Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) has a question and I will allow her to ask it.

I point out to my hon. friends that this matter is under very active consideration in Ontario where it has been referred to the Ontario Law Reform Commission. In fact, they have had very short notice and will be preparing a report for the Ontario Government some time in May. The Ontario Government, with the support of the NDP in the Ontario Legislature, as a result of the accord between those two Parties, has undertaken to take early action on the matter of expanding political rights for provincial public employees. The question is whether we will forever be bogged down with this issue or whether action will be taken.
Let me also point out that this is a matter of importance to those of us who represent members of the Public Service of Canada not only because of a pending election in 1988 or 1989 but because it is posing a real dilemma for employees of the Public Service of Canada. Yesterday I received a phone call from an individual who has returned to the Public Service after taking leave and is now under great pressure to abandon his activities within the riding association of a political Party. He is identified in the community as being part of that political Party because he was a candidate in an election.
There is no law stipulating that he should not be part of a riding executive between election campaigns but the pressure is there, with no clear definition of his rights and responsibilities apart from the guidelines issued by the Public Service Commission. However, the court has determined that these guidelines have no legal effect. Nevertheless, these guidelines apply in terms of disciplinary action by his employer.
Let me read into the record a specific promise which was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was campaigning for office in 1984. In a letter to Mr. Jack Donegani, who was then President of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, the Prime Minister, then Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, stated:
We believe that this matter-
The matter of political rights for federal employees:
-should be addressed by an all-Party Parliamentary Committee in consultation with public service organizations and we believe the situation can be quickly resolved. Much of the work, after all has been done as part of the D'Avignon Report, but the current Government has not demonstrated the political will necessary to implement the long overdue changes.
I do not always agree with the Prime Minister, but with regard to what he said to the Professional Institute in August, 1984, I am entirely in agreement. The former Liberal Government lacked the political will. The reform in terms of granting political rights to Public Service employees is long overdue. While Members from different sides of the House may have somewhat different ideas about exactly what should occur-I believe there is harmony-its consideration is surely long overdue.
I have been proposing that this matter go before a parliamentary committee since last April so that the issue could get on the rails rather than being side-tracked as appears to have been the case due to other priorities of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and the Government.

February 7, 1986
Public Service
As the Prime Minister indicated a couple of years ago, the matter can be quickly resolved if there is the political will to do so. It is up to Members of the House to demonstrate that we have the political will to act. This question has long been a priority of the unions representing federal Public Service employees and they have indicated their support for quick parliamentary action on political rights.
I am somewhat disappointed that the Conservative Government has failed in its efforts to fulfil promises to Public Service unions so far. However, this is not a costly issue and involves a categorical promise made by the Government. For that reason I suggest we can send this question to a committee and allow it to come back with a report and recommendations that would expedite this matter.
Members are aware that there is a group of Public Service employees who are taking this issue to court in April. I have some association with that case but, frankly, I would prefer to see the matter settled by Parliament before going through such court procedures. I believe this matter can be decided in Parliament.
I also point out that the Equality Now report issued by a committee of this House gave a clear recommendation in favour of giving political rights to public employees. Members will recall that the committee considered representations from myself, the Public Service Alliance and others. Let me quote from the Equality Now report under the heading "Political Rights of Public Servants". It reads:
All Canadian citizens have the right to take part in the political process of their country. Freedom of expression and freedom of association are enshrined in section 2 of the Charter. The democratic right to vote and to serve as a candidate in provincial and federal elections is also recognized in section 3 of the Charter. The law does recognize a number of legitimate restrictions on these broadly state rights. Concern was expressed in several submissions to the Committee about the limitations on the political rights of federal public servants.
Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act forbids public servants from "working for, on behalf of or against" a political party or candidate for election to the House of Commons or a provincial or territorial legislature. Federal public servants subject to the Act are also barred from being candidates in such elections unless they obtain a leave of absence from the Public Service Commission. The participation of public servants in the political process is limited to voting, contributing funds to a political party or candidate and attending meetings. If a public servant engages in activities prohibited under Section 32, he or she can be dismissed by the Public Service Commission upon inquiry after a complaint is made by a candidate or former candidate for election.
This has been said many times. It is significant that, despite the fact that that law has been on the books for almost 20 years, no such complaint has, in fact, ever been launched with the Public Service Commission. In other words, we and our predecessor Members and all those men and women who ran as candidates have never ourselves been offended by the participation of federal public employees in election campaigns. As the Hon. Member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) and my other colleague from the Ottawa area know, I do think a few federal employees have taken part in campaigns.
The Equality Now subcommittee report goes on to state:
While we believe that the political neutrality of the public service must be preserved as a general principle, it seems to us that the rights of public servants are, at least in certain circumstances, unduly curtailed. The prohibition against campaigning, soliciting funds and assuming official functions with a political party applies to all public servants, even to those whose job classifications are such that no suspicion of conflict of interest or breach of trust might arise from the exercise of such political rights.
Again, that echoes some comments made in the D'Avignon Report which tried to draw the distinction between the 4,000 or 5,000 senior members of the Public Service who clearly exercise policy making or policy development functions on the one hand and, on the other hand, a large number of people who work as nurses, draftspeople, truck drivers, et cetera who clearly are not in a position to influence policy, were they to indulge in apparently partisan activities.
The recommendation of the Equality Rights Subcommittee reads:
We recommend that Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act be amended to ensure that no greater limitations are imposed on the political rights of public servants than are necessary to maintain a politically neutral public service.
I would have liked to have seen a little stronger recommendation, but nonetheless I think that is a challenge put out to the rest of us in this House by the Equality Rights Subcommittee. I think it is something on which we are in a position to act in view of the promise made by the Prime Minister.
Just what does that mean? The Equality Rights Subcommittee had to look at a vast range of other matters as well. It dealt with political rights only in one paragraph or two and in that one recommendation. I believe this is a matter which affects 250,000 federal public employees. Indirectly it affects some 600,000 people working for Governments at different levels across Canada. I do believe it is important for the Government of Canada to try to give a lead.
I will conclude my remarks so that other Members can have a chance to contribute to the debate. Since September 4, 1984, we have heard more about political rights for federal employees in this House than I think we had in a century before that. This has been good, the matter has been ventilated, and it is being raised. Now I believe it is time for all of us in all three Parties to implement the commitment that our Parties gave in the 1984 election, which was to take action on political rights so that before the 1988 election, hopefully sooner than that, federal employees can have the kind of rights that I think would be in the spirit of the report of the Equality Rights Subcommittee, of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and of what most other democratic jurisdictions give to their Public Service employees, that is, with very narrow restrictions, that civil servants can be treated like any other citizens of this country when it comes to political rights.
I urge my colleagues on all sides of the House to support the amendment and then to send this out to a Commons committee for a report by the end of June, 1986.

Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the opportunity on behalf of my constituents in Nepean-
February 7, 1986

Carleton to rise this afternoon and offer some comments on the amendments before the House to the motion moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), respecting political rights of public servants.
I think we should congratulate my colleague from Ottawa Centre on his interest in extending the political rights of public servants. He has been an advocate of it while a member of the provincial legislature in the Province of Ontario, and an advocate of it in a very aggressive and thoughtful way since he has taken his seat in this House. He was particularly involved with the matter during the 1984 election campaign.
I think we should take note that the Hon. Member represents the federal riding of Ottawa Centre. This House should be cognizant of the fact that his predecessor from that riding was in many ways instrumental in delaying legislation relative to the extension of the political rights of public servants during the course of the previous Parliament.
I think every Government, regardless of its political stripe, requires at its side a strong Public Service, a competent Public Service, a contemporary and willing Public Service and one that is loyal.
The Public Service I know is that kind of Public Service. The people who work in the Department of Energy Mines and Resources, the Department of Agriculture, the National Research Council, and the Department of Communications are the ones with whom I am familiar in more detail, but that group of men and women are world class. I am sure the expertise they have can be found in all of the Departments across the Public Service.
I need to acknowledge, in all fairness, that during the 1984 election campaign, the political rights of public servants was widely discussed in my own riding. I was disappointed, to be fair about it, when a lot of my close personal friends, people who were neighbours, people who had worked with me in municipal campaigns earlier, were unable to become involved in my federal nomination or in my federal election campaign. In a way, they became political eunuchs. Much of the threatening aspect to them was derived from a communication issued in February, 1984, over the signature of Edgar Gallant and two other commissioners from the Public Service Commission who gave their interpretation of Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act. I found that Mr. Gallant and his commissioners' interpretation of that section was an enormously conservative interpretation of the guidelines. I think it forced in the 1984 election a large number of public servants, who might well have qualified under Section 32 to participate in some way in the political process, to withdraw from it. Because of that, the concern over Section 32 and the limitation on political rights of public servants was therefore highlighted.
What did our Party say about political rights? In many respects the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre correctly quoted the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in his communications about political rights. The Progressive Conservative Party, in responding to the professional institute, as
Public Service
was noted earlier, indicated that it favoured a general removal of the restrictions on political activities, especially for those public servants covered by collective agreements. These restrictions are unnecessary and may not be justifiable under the terms of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. There are probably some senior public servants whose job responsibilities are very political in nature and whose rights should be somewhat restricted to prevent conflict of interest, but we are confident that these people could be covered separately, without disenfranchising over 200,000 public servants in the process.
You know, Mr. Speaker, where the Prime Minister and my Party stand on this particular issue. I personally favour in style that recommendations which were put forward in the D'Avig-non Report. It is a concept which is fairly widely used in the British House of Commons and in the British Parliament, where public servants are in fact tiered. For example, there is a tier of persons who have total political freedoms and an upper tier of those who do not. In between there is a tier of people whose political activities can be structured in the framework to varying degrees. The system seems to work reasonably well. We should look at that model very carefully. There is one aspect about it which I find attractive. It is that the public servant knows, when he accepts a certain class of employment within the Public Service, what political rights he has at the time of engagement. There might be some difficulty in the initial moments, but I am sure that sort of thing can be phased in without a great deal of difficulty.
The issue of the right of public servants to participate in political activities has been with us for a long time. With the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, we, as defenders of the rights of the individual, will have to make a decision quickly on the political rights of those who provide counsel to the Government. At issue is the fundamental relationship of the Canadian political system, with Parliament at its core, to the federal Public Service.
Canadians have a tradition going back many generations of being able to approach public servants without having to consider their political affiliation, or that of the public servant with whom they deal, and how it might make a difference in their treatment. I am proud of that tradition, as I think are all Canadians. In that regard we have set a world standard. I hold our Public Service in the same high standard as observers from foreign lands who have seen and studied the systems and operations both here and in other countries. For those individuals working in the Public Service, the present situation offers them perhaps the best career opportunities in Canada, where advancement is based firmly on the principle of merit, not on whom one knows, not on one's political connections, not on buying one's way to the top with influence or wealth. Canada has stubbornly rejected the American system of "across the board" high-level purges and firings when a new administration is voted into office. The Canadian Public Service has been impartial and, equally important, has been seen to be impartial since Confederation. A very notable thing happened in 1984 when in this country we had a democratic

February 7, 1986
Public Service
revolution. There was no political purge of the Public Service. I hope all Canadians and all Members of the House take note of that.
The very creation of a management category in the federal Public Service is predicated upon the goal of encouraging professionalism, merit and impartiality in the category of senior managers charged with effectively delivering needed Government programs to Canadians in all regions of the country. That falls into two parts-the creation of policy or offering policy alternatives to be decided upon by persons in the House and then, once decided upon, their delivery across the nation.
A great deal of energy and expense has gone into honing the skills of these fine and capable men and women, the majority of whom, from my experience, are genuinely instilled with a desire to be of true public service. Are we to clean shop every time a new Government is elected? What a waste. Nevertheless, a Public Service with certain political rights and freedoms is clearly an idea whose time has come. Which of the many issues in today's complex and whirlwind society that profoundly affect Canadians has not sorely tempted all Canadian citizens, including those who might happen to work in the federal Public Service, to voice their opinions to friends, to co-workers, to editors of newspapers, to their clergy and, perhaps more important, to their Members of Parliament? When is this hypothetical public servant about whom I speak to be considered as criticizing his or her employer on any of these issues? When does freedom of expression become political activity? By responding to a heartfelt emotion and appearing in a peace march? By reacting with honest emotion and concern over the shooting of a police officer and writing to a Member of Parliament about reinstating capital punishment? Which of today's pressing issues does not touch, at least in some way, the mandate of one of the hundreds of federal Government Departments, programs or agencies?
Surely it is obvious that a case can be made that almost any issue one cares to name falls in some way under federal jurisdiction. Common sense tells us that the issue of political rights of public servants is far more encompassing and pervasive than just the freedom to criticize politically the "employer". Have we really sounded out the views of public servants in an adequate fashion? Has the consultative process been complete? Do we fully understand whether public servants want to be involved and want to have total political rights?
In any case, the matter warrants serious examination. It should be studied, ideally it seems to me, in a respected and existing forum in which representatives of both the employer and employees can air their views constructively, suggest and discuss approaches, and arrive at a mutually agreeable course of action for consideration by the House.
Another reason that the time has come for the granting of certain specific political rights and privileges to public servants is that there is a great deal of intellect, expertise and ability to be found in the ranks of public servants. My constituents, many of them people of logic, compassion and talent, of all political stripes, make this Chamber the worthy institution
that is it. The federal Public Service, from my experience, has a large share of that kind of person. The Public Service is a great resource to the country, not just as a large employer. In it can be found men and women of great distinction who work in many cases far harder than many people in the private sector. It is a shame not to be making better use of this resource. We have sitting Members in the House who are veterinarians, pharmacists, lawyers, chartered accountants, why not public servants? Certain constituencies, particularly around the National Capital Region, are assured of having residing in their midst future Mike Pearsons or John Diefen-bakers with a great contribution to make to their country. Not just individual ridings, but the Parliament of Canada would be better served if these people could be brought into this House by the voters to share their gifts and participate in the free political process as all Canadians can.
The Government has every hope that this will soon be a reality and that the basic provisions contained in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms can be realized by as many public servants as possible. However, if we work hard enough and are smart enough, with adequate consultation with affected parties, which has been an overriding principle of this Government since it has been elected, the final result should be a Bill of enduring value and a real credit to all Members of this House. Only then should a fully thought-out piece of legislation be presented for debate and consideration, with all clauses having been thoroughly thought through in their scope and in their immediate and long-term implications, and without political impartiality entering into it.
I welcome the opportunity to share with the House some of my thoughts on the issue of political rights for public servants, on the need for this Parliament to provide public servants with much needed access to the political process, so they are not political eunuchs in the future. I very much hope that in the days ahead all of my colleagues will be able, in a unanimous fashion, to endorse legislation that will extend the political rights of public servants over and beyond what they now enjoy. Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.

Anyway, Mr. Speaker, the basic premise behind the principle of neutrality is one of trust, a trust that the Public Service has earned from both the Government and the Canadian public. It has earned the trust from the Government because of a reputation for offering advice that is untainted by partisan or political bias. This tradition goes back

February 7, 1986
Public Service
to the beginning of this century when laws were enacted to guarantee the neutrality of the Public Service. They were passed to ensure that it would not be used as a political tool by Governments and that Public Service positions would not be filled through patronage to further the cause of one political Party.
I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on Private Members' Hour on behalf of myself, because that is what Private Members' hour is all about. It allows Members of Parliament to bring forth issues that are of importance to them. While we are extending the rights and privileges to public servants, there is one thing that must not be overlooked, and this has to do with an experience I personally had during the last federal election. A chief executive officer of one of the unions was a candidate for the constituency of Red Deer. He was funded partially by union dues. This was not fair to the members of that union because they had no choice as to whether or not they should pay their dues. They had to pay those dues in order to hold down their jobs. Of course, those dues or a portion of them went to support a candidate that was not of their choice.
When we are talking about political freedoms for the Public Service, I think we are going to have to take a serious look at that aspect of the matter. If the members of the union to which I was referring had paid dues of their own free will, I would not have any problem with this. However, they did not have any choice. They were forced to pay those dues and, as all Hon. Members know, those dues are quite substantial in a great many cases. When they are used for political purposes against the wishes of the union members to support a candidate not of their choice, I consider that to be an injustice and on of the things at which we must look when talking about giving civil servants freedoms.
Canadians expect as a right to be served in an impartial manner without consideration of their political beliefs or opinions. That right is a fact under the present regulations which ensure the political neutrality of the Public Service. The trust Canadians have in the Public Service extends to the Government, and it is conceivable that should citizens lose their confidence in the impartiality and neutrality of the Public Service, they may well lose their confidence in the Government.
The concept of neutrality extends to public servants themselves. Current regulations ensure that their careers and advancement are dictated by the merit principle. They are guaranteed protection from unfair or arbitrary dismissal or capricious career decisions due to political beliefs. This protection permits them to accomplish their responsibilities free from the fear that they may be subject to reprisals from new political leaders.
The last few years have brought a great many changes to the perceptions of individual rights and the balance between the rights and regulations governing the political rights of public servants. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees freedom of expression and of association for all Canadians, and that includes public servants. However, reasonable limitations must remain to ensure the impartiality and maintain the integrity of the Public Service. These limitations are required particularly in respect of those who are responsible for advising or counselling the Government on policy matters.
In examining the rights of public servants, we must not lose sight of the basic principle which I stated earlier, it being the trust that exists between the Canadian public and the Public Service. Whatever direction is finally decided upon must ensure that the confidence that has been developed be maintained and whatever trust exists between the Ministers and the Public Service must be protected to guarantee the impartiality of Government actions and programs.
I propose to the House that it would be unwise to proceed with the proposed Bill since it is the Government's firm intention to come to an understanding with the unions that would satisfy all parties and would deal with the aspect of this matter to which I referred a moment ago. I am sure all Hon. Members would agree that a solution should be arrived at that is mutually satisfactory.
In conclusion, let me reiterate that this Party has always believed that the best way to solve important issues facing the Government is to discuss them with the interested parties and to seek a mutually satisfactory agreement that this issue should be resolved in this manner. I know that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Cadieux), has something he wishes to put before you at this time, Mr. Speaker.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It is not easy to speak out when the Hon. Member is here, but I will try, in spite of her efforts to prevent the House and the Canadian public from hearing, to make my views known so that we may have the opinion of everybody about this important Bill. People, whether or not they belong to the Public Service, have basic rights which should be respected, but I believe we should look into the issue before accepting anything blindly as some would have us. Perhaps I should refer to my notes so that I won't put my foot in it. I shall continue by saying that the issue of political rights for civil servants deserves to be seriously and thoroughly examined. As a matter of fact, it is an issue which is raised each time there is an election, whether on the federal, provincial or municipal level. Thus a good many of us during the last election campaign, had to discuss the matter with our constituents to determine under what circumstances public servants could actively take part in the political process and when they should refrain from doing so.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the Public Service should remain neutral as far as politics are concerned. If not, its credibility in the eyes of the Canadian public which it is called upon to serve would be jeopardized. Moreover, the Public Service Employment Act now in effect is there to ensure a certain degree of neutrality during election campaigns
Public Service
by restricting political activities of public servants. Thus the Act provides as follows and I quote:
No employee shall
(a) engage in work for, on behalf of or against a candidate ... or engage in
work for, on behalf of or against a political party;
However, this legislation provides that an employee does not contravene the legislation when he attends a political meeting or contributes to a candidate's fund. Moreover, public servants can stand as candidates to an election provided that they have previously obtained leave without pay for such a purpose.
Clearly, in the discharge of his responsibilities a Deputy Minister has to avoid any political partisanship. This is selfevident, Mr. Speaker, and of course there must be neutrality if operations are not to become very difficult, whatever the Government or the official concerned. To the same extent, various other officials must be absolutely neutral as regards Government policy. Indeed, when the Public Service Commission considers an application for leave submitted by any official wishing to be a candidate in an election, it takes into account the employee's group and level, to preclude any doubt in the public's mind as to the possibility of the official involved being in a conflict of interest situation.
Such a neutrality, which has been a tradition ever since the turn of the century and accepted as a rule, is viewed by some people as contrary to the basic principle of the rights and freedoms of public servants. An increasing number of people seem to share that view, especially since 1982, when the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms was proclaimed. The Charter guarantees freedom of expression and, I believe, even for Members of Parliament, the freedom of thought, belief and opinion for all Canadians, and of course federal civil servants for that matter.
We should therefore look at the nature and scope of the limitations imposed upon civil servants in the area of freedom of expression and association. Perhaps we should even question the concept that they do not enjoy the freedom of speech in matters political and that they must seriously restrain their activities in that area.
Any restriction to the rights as enshrined in the Charter must be justifiable. Any change made to the provisions dealing with federal civil servants must both be in line with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and take heed of the concept of political neutrality in the Public Service. Any scrutiny of the matter of the right civil servants have to take part in political life must keep a fair balance between the rights of civil servants in light of the Charter on the one hand, and the neutrality of the Public Service on the other.
To the extent that we can safeguard the impartiality of the Public Service, the Government shares the view that the restrictions now in force concerning political activities of public servants should be mitigated. However, caution should be exercized in that respect, because it would be unacceptable,

Mr. Speaker, to jeopardize the neutrality of the Public Service. This would involve reconsidering the concept of a permanent public service operating on the merit principle, a public service capable of serving the Government of the day with great objectivity and in line with the best interests of the Canadian people. Some questions remain-for instance, would a highly politically involved public servant still be in a position to provide the Government with his best advice? Could he remain objective and impartial? Would that same public servant be protected against arbitrary decisions that might affect his career? Could he be guaranteed that his promotions would be based on the merit principle?
Would he be protected against an unjustified discharge? It seems difficult to believe so, Mr. Speaker.
The Federal public servant knows that his future does not depend on the political party in power. He knows that the merit principle gives him some security. He has some means of redress as concerns decisions which affect his career. Perhaps because of these reasons, he may not wish to question the principle of his exclusion from the political scene, but is this a reason to refuse this right to the entire Public Service?
In any case, any examination of the neutrality of the Public Service and the right of public servants to take part in political activities will have to be made in consultation with the unions and will have to take into account public opinion on the matter.
Mr. Speaker, the Government is convinced that a proper balance can be reached in this area. Moreover, the Government will do everything possible to attain this balance.
